source.title: SafeAnchor: Preventing Cumulative Safety Erosion in Continual Domain Adaptation of Large Language Models
source.authors: Dong-Xing Guo; Ji-Kun Wu; Siu-Ming Yiu

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether ordinary domain fine-tuning erodes safety using sequential adaptation and composite safety scores, and evaluates whether a low-rank LoRA safety subspace can help preserve it. It does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or first-token measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior findings about shallow alignment, benign fine-tuning, and adversarial examples; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its own relevant results concern sequential domain adaptation, Fisher-based LoRA subspaces, and GCG suffix robustness. It does not measure per-token KL, compliant prefills, or decoding changes.
record.test_reason: Unconstrained sequential LoRA fine-tuning on ordinary domain data (MedQA, LegalBench, CodeAlpaca) cuts the composite safety score on two chat models. That bears on V2 in a new multi-domain sequential setting. The rest of the paper evaluates the authors' mitigation method.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that sequential domain adaptation causes compounding safety erosion (Standard LoRA loses 47.8 points). They say SafeAnchor retains about 93% of original safety, beats baselines by 18–42 points, and stays within 1.5 points of unconstrained LoRA on domain tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates sequential domain-specific LoRA fine-tuning with Fisher-subspace constraints and safety monitoring, rather than testing the cited small-scale harmful or benign fine-tuning interventions or measuring first-token concentration.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary with adaptation method, domain ordering, ρ, τ, calibration-set size Ns, and repair-step count. GCG attack results vary across adaptation methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Fisher information of LoRA gradients on a safety calibration set is concentrated in about 8 eigenvectors per layer, versus a near-flat spectrum on random training data. Projecting task gradients away from this subspace keeps composite safety at 79.6 versus 43.6 for unconstrained LoRA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-relevant gradient directions in LoRA parameter space are low-rank, and protecting them limits safety erosion during benign fine-tuning.

record.problems: The main safety measure is a composite of refusal, truthfulness, and bias rather than harmful-compliance rate alone. The GCG results have no matched no-suffix refusal-rate comparison, and use a compute-reduced attack configuration that the authors say yields higher absolute refusal rates than full-budget GCG. Experiments focus on 7B models and a primary three-domain sequence.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results omitted. Domain-task and general-capability scores were left out because they do not measure a claim version.

untested.parts: No small-dataset or carefully selected benign data. No HarmBench refusal rate reported separately from the composite.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill or decoding attacks. The GCG attack lacks a no-attack or unadapted baseline.
No test that a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behaviour; only a Fisher subspace of LoRA gradients is examined.

missing.what: Standard LoRA composite safety continues to fall: 32.7 after a fourth domain, 24.9 after a fifth.
Standard LoRA final composite safety across all six domain orderings: 40.5–44.9.
WildGuard jailbreak robustness after Standard LoRA: 38.7 ± 3.1. No base-model value is given.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 limits_scope label (SafeAnchor rows) and V5 labels were dropped: they rest on the study's own mitigation method versus baselines, not on whether the claim holds. The V4 GCG rows have no matched no-suffix or base-model refusal rate, so they cannot show the suffix's effect. Original sources are only cited.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning intervention or few-to-hundreds-of-examples sweep.

Tests sequential domain fine-tuning and reports a composite safety score, not harmful-compliance rates alone. Does not test small datasets or carefully selected benign examples as a separate condition.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
Tests GCG-style adversarial suffixes only. No compliant-prefill or decoding-change experiment.
Tests Fisher-defined low-rank directions in LoRA parameter space, not whether a small set of ordinary model weights or ranks generally carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether the data or objective causes safety to be shallow across response tokens.
Does not train or evaluate safety spread beyond the first response tokens.

labels.condition: Unconstrained sequential LoRA domain fine-tuning (Medical→Legal→Code), Llama-2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct
labels.reason: r1, r9, r15 and r16 report a composite of HarmBench refusal, TruthfulQA and inverted BBQ. Component results are not separated, so these declines cannot establish the increase in harmful compliance V2 specifies.

relation.reason: The study reports its own safety-subspace validation relevant to V5, rather than only assuming or citing localization. Its composite-score results do not separately establish increased harmful compliance under V2.

tranche.reason: Sequential multi-domain adaptation is a new setting. The study also empirically examines low-rank safety subspaces relevant to V5 in Section 4.4 and Appendix D; the listed composite rows do not establish V2.

source_check.notes: Both statements accurately describe this study, including the composite-measure caveat, but their accuracy does not justify the V2 verdict. Section 4.4's low-rank safety-subspace validation is relevant to V5 and is not represented by the listed rows.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard sequential domain fine-tuning on Llama-2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct
reader_labels.reason: The composite safety score falls from 91.4 to 43.6 and from 88.7 to 39.2 after Standard LoRA adaptation (r1, r9); the Llama trajectory also declines at successive stages (r15, r16).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Fine-tuning does not erase the composite score to the same degree under these methods; SafeAnchor ends at 85.2 on Llama-2-7B-Chat and 82.6 on Mistral-7B-Instruct (r8, r14).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GCG suffix attacks on the tested adapted baselines
reader_labels.reason: Several adapted baselines show low refusal rates under the suffix attack, including Standard LoRA at 31.2 ± 3.8 (r17).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: SafeAnchor retains 78.4 ± 2.1% refusal under the tested attack, so the suffix does not eliminate refusal in this condition (r24).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fisher-defined safety subspace in LoRA parameter space and SafeAnchor ablations
reader_labels.reason: The safety-calibration Fisher spectrum is low-rank, and gradient projection substantially improves the reported safety score over Standard LoRA (r25, r28, r29, r31).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SSI alone and removal of incremental SSI updating
reader_labels.reason: SSI without projection has minimal effect, and omitting incremental updating lowers the full-method score by 5.1 points (r27, r32).
